Washington’s Absence Is Inviting the War Europe Fears Most

Renewed U.S. leadership in the pushback against Russia is crucial to avoiding catastrophe.

By David Ignatius, a columnist for the Washington Post.

Here’s the scenario of a war game played Monday by a group of current members of Congress and former U.S. military, diplomatic, and intelligence officials. It’s 2028, the Ukraine war remains a bloody stalemate, and Russia sees a chance to further splinter Europe by attacking Moldova. One of its drones hits a fuel depot in Romania, a NATO member, killing civilians.

What does the United States do? The answer in this simulation, as I fear would be the case in real life, was a tepid response—and an implicit statement that NATO’s Article 5 pledge of collective security is almost a dead letter. In the simulation, the members of Congress agreed that the American public wouldn’t support strong action. And without U.S. leadership, Europe would be fragmented and disorganized.

What does the United States do? The answer in this simulation, as I fear would be the case in real life, was a tepid response—and an implicit statement that NATO’s Article 5 pledge of collective security is almost a dead letter. In the simulation, the members of Congress agreed that the American public wouldn’t support strong action. And without U.S. leadership, Europe would be fragmented and disorganized.
Welcome to World War Next. The simulation, co-sponsored by Cornell University’s Brooks Institute and the Rockefeller Foundation, was the clearest demonstration I’ve seen that the framework that has protected U.S. and European security for 81 years is crumbling, as shared military and diplomatic tools disappear. And the worst of it is that President Donald Trump is part of the demolition team. (I attended the simulation and was allowed to report on it as long as I didn’t identify participants.)
The grim fact is that Russia’s war on Ukraine is escalating and spreading to NATO countries. That’s a new reality that most Americans (including many senior Trump administration officials) don’t seem to recognize. Russia’s “hybrid” war against European supporters of Ukraine is moving from the gray zone to blood red, and the United States is doing little to deter the attacks.
“Russian hybrid activity in Europe became more ambitious and dangerous” over the past six months, according to a private analysis shared with me by TD International, a Washington-based strategic advisory firm. TDI analysts counted 63 Russia-linked incidents against European targets since March, including 43 drone or other airspace incidents, six sabotage operations or plots, six cyber or electronic-warfare attacks and five hostile maritime incidents.
This escalation against Europe, matched by more intense Russian missile attacks on Kyiv, is President Vladimir Putin’s answer to arguments that he’s losing the Ukraine war. “One does not negotiate with terrorists,” Putin snapped early Wednesday, just days after CIA Director John Ratcliffe visited Moscow and warned his Russian counterparts that the war was at an impasse.
Ratcliffe traveled to Moscow because he and top U.S. diplomats and military commanders felt that Putin wasn’t getting an accurate assessment of Russia’s battlefield problems, according to a knowledgeable official. The hope was that talks between intelligence officials might open a more realistic path to ceasefire discussions than those conducted by Trump’s emissaries, businessmen Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff, which haven’t budged the Russian leader. Some officials hoped Ratcliffe would also warn against Russian hybrid attacks on NATO countries, but he didn’t press that topic, said several officials, who requested anonymity because of the sensitivity of the issues.
Putin’s prompt rejection of the Ratcliffe message has been evident in the nearly round-the-clock missile attacks on Kyiv in recent days. And on Wednesday, he rejected alternatives to the Kushner-Witkoff channel, saying: “We are perfectly comfortable working with people we know well and whom we generally trust – individuals close to President Trump.”
Facing an implacable Putin and a Ukrainian population increasingly hunkered down in shelters, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky this week threatened his own escalation. “We want to warn every airline that uses Russian airspace, every insurer, and everyone who still uses Russia’s key airports [that] Russian airspace is becoming completely unsafe” because of Ukrainian drones. Putin quickly denounced this threat as “state terrorism.”
What makes the situation so dangerous now is that Putin is clearly trying to regain the advantage by attacking the European nations that have become Ukraine’s main weapons suppliers. In April, Russia’s Defense Ministry published the names and addresses of 21 companies in Europe it claimed were producing drones or parts for Kyiv, and officials warned that they were “potential targets.”

Trump and the Iran war gave Russia a boost. Brussels is fed up.

Russian attacks on these European arms suppliers have followed. A summary last week by the Daily Telegraph noted August sabotage attacks on Milrem Robotics in Estonia, which provides drones to Ukraine; EMCO in Bulgaria, which sells 155mm artillery shells; and KNDS Ammo in Italy, which provides munitions. Many of these attacks have been conducted by local criminal gangs, avoiding Russian GRU fingerprints.
Germany this week accused Russia of an Aug. 4 drone attack on a Ukrainian cargo plane at Leipzig/Halle airport and two other attempted drone strikes. The German foreign minister said the Leipzig strike was part of “a long chain” of Russian attacks, and the interior minister said, “We are the daily target of hybrid warfare.” Germany took diplomatic measures against Russia and warned it would increase surveillance of the shadow fleet that secretly exports Russian oil.
Britain, which has faced more than a year of Russian sabotage and arson, has pushed for a more muscular response. Andy Burnham, Britain’s new prime minister, visited Kyiv last week and announced that Britain would join France in helping Ukraine build an advanced cruise missile, known in Britain as Storm Shadow and in France as SCALP. A Kremlin spokesman said Britain was “hell bent on pouring oil on a fire,” to which Burnham retorted: “Who started the fire?”
As Europe and Russia mount the escalation ladder, what can the United States do to prevent catastrophe? The answer is simple: The United States should once again act like a superpower and the leader of the transatlantic alliance.
Here are some specific steps the Trump administration could take to deter Putin and reassure America’s European allies, drawn from my recent conversations with senior military and intelligence officials and politicians.
The United States should first issue a joint statement with its European allies bluntly warning that continued Kremlin-sponsored strikes on NATO countries will result in severe consequences. And if Putin continues nonstop attacks on Ukrainian cities, the United States and Europe should quietly assist Ukraine in proportional attacks on Russia.
To bolster the NATO alliance, the Pentagon should immediately pause its review of U.S. military deployments in Europe. This is no time to be debating removing troops. Trump has already invoked the Defense Production Act to rebuild America’s arsenal. Some of that increased production should be available for Europe and Ukraine to purchase.
And finally, as Trump strengthens the hand of Ukraine and Europe, he should use that leverage to find an endgame for this terrible war before it consumes that continent—by gaining the ceasefire and eventual peace he has rightly sought since he became president.
The danger of letting the current situation slide isn’t simply the failure to deter Putin but a growing inability to restrain European allies who feel abandoned and increasingly desperate. The advantage of U.S. military strength isn’t just to make war but to stop it.
